Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.summary: An ionic solid is a three-dimensional electrostatic lattice whose stability reflects ion charges, sizes and lattice enthalpy.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.mistake: Do not answer Ionic bonding and lattice enthalpy from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.application: Ionic bonding and lattice enthalpy supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.explanation: Born-Haber cycles combine formation, atomisation, ionisation, electron-gain and lattice enthalpies using Hess's law. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.example: Example: MgO has much larger lattice enthalpy than NaCl because its ions carry charges of magnitude two and have strong attraction. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result.

Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.summary: A metal's position in the reactivity series determines whether it is extracted by electrolysis, chemical reduction or heating of its ore.
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.mistake: Do not propose carbon reduction for sodium or aluminium oxides; these metals are more reactive than carbon.
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.application: Selecting extraction routes balances chemical feasibility, energy demand, ore composition, pollution control and recycling.
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.explanation: Highly reactive K-Ca-Na-Mg-Al metals require electrolysis of molten compounds. Middle metals such as Zn, Fe, Pb and Cu are commonly obtained after converting ores to oxides and reducing with carbon/CO or aluminium. Low-reactivity metals may occur native or be recovered by heating.
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.relationship: high activity -> electrolysis; middle -> roasting/calcination then reduction; low -> heating or native occurrence
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.example: Example: ZnS is roasted: 2ZnS + 3O2 -> 2ZnO + 2SO2; then ZnO + C -> Zn + CO. Aluminium oxide instead requires molten electrolysis.

Gases.summary: Gases have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.
Gases.mistake: A gas does not have zero mass; its low density simply makes its mass less obvious.
Gases.application: Gas behavior is used in breathing equipment, tyres, refrigeration and weather forecasting.
Gases.explanation: Gas particles are far apart, move rapidly in random directions and have weak attractions, so a gas fills its container and is easily compressed.
Gases.relationship: far-apart fast particles -> diffusion + high compressibility
Gases.example: Example: perfume molecules spread through a room by diffusion, showing that gas particles move and mix.

Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.summary: Soap ions have a water-attracting ionic head and an oil-attracting hydrocarbon tail, allowing them to surround grease in micelles.
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.mistake: Do not say soap chemically destroys all grease; its principal cleansing action emulsifies and suspends oily material.
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.application: Micelles enable washing, emulsification and formulation of cleaners and personal-care products.
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.explanation: Above a suitable concentration in water, tails cluster inward around oily dirt while charged heads face outward. Agitation breaks grease into suspended droplets that can be rinsed away.
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.relationship: hydrophobic tails -> grease core; hydrophilic COO- heads -> water
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.example: Example: When oily cloth is washed with soap, micelles encapsulate oil and keep droplets dispersed instead of redepositing them on the fabric.

Undergraduate|Materials Chemistry|Cerami.summary: Ceramics are inorganic nonmetallic materials processed by shaping and high-temperature densification.
Undergraduate|Materials Chemistry|Cerami.mistake: Do not treat Ceramics as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Undergraduate|Materials Chemistry|Cerami.application: This concept connects processing and molecular structure with useful mechanical, electrical, optical or biological performance.
Undergraduate|Materials Chemistry|Cerami.explanation: At undergraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Materials Chemistry, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Undergraduate|Materials Chemistry|Cerami.example: Example: Sintering an alumina compact reduces porosity and raises strength without fully melting the body.

Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.summary: Valence-bond theory forms covalent bonds by overlap of half-filled atomic orbitals with opposite-spin electron pairing.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.mistake: Do not answer Valence-bond theory from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.application: Valence-bond theory supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.explanation: Overlap magnitude affects strength and directionality, but simple valence-bond theory alone cannot explain every magnetic observation. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.relationship: head-on overlap -> sigma; side-on overlap -> pi
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.example: Example: In N2, one sigma and two pi overlaps create a triple bond. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result.

Precision.summary: Precision describes how closely repeated measurements agree with one another.
Precision.mistake: Precision does not guarantee accuracy. Check the definition, particles and evidence before deciding.
Precision.application: Precision is important when checking whether a manufacturing or laboratory method gives consistent results.
Precision.explanation: A precise set has little spread, but it may still be far from the accepted value if a systematic problem affects every reading.
Precision.example: Example: 9.81, 9.82 and 9.81 g are more precise than 9.3, 10.1 and 9.7 g. This illustrates the key relationship; explain the particles or quantities involved and keep all symbols and units consistent.

Thermodynamics|Internal energy.summary: Internal energy is the total microscopic kinetic and potential energy of a system.
Thermodynamics|Internal energy.mistake: Do not omit the sign of work or assume internal energy depends only on temperature for every system.
Thermodynamics|Internal energy.application: Internal-energy balances are used in reactors, engines, batteries and phase-change equipment.
Thermodynamics|Internal energy.explanation: Its absolute value is usually unknown, but changes can be measured. The first law says energy changes through heat and work and is conserved overall.
Thermodynamics|Internal energy.example: Example: if a system absorbs 300 J of heat and 80 J of work is done on it, deltaU = 300 + 80 = 380 J.

Statistical mechanics.summary: Statistical mechanics connects molecular energy levels and populations with bulk thermodynamic properties.
Statistical mechanics.explanation: Connects molecular energy levels and populations with bulk thermodynamic properties.
Statistical mechanics.example: For two states separated by deltaE, their equilibrium population ratio is exp(-deltaE/kT) when degeneracies are equal.

Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds|Preparatio.summary: Carboxylic acids form by oxidation or hydrolysis and react through acidity and nucleophilic acyl substitution to make salts, esters, acyl halides and amides.
Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds|Preparatio.mistake: Do not confuse alcohol acidity with carboxylic-acid acidity or forget that Fischer esterification is an equilibrium requiring acid catalyst.
Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds|Preparatio.application: Carboxylic-acid derivatives occur in medicines, polymers, food preservatives, fats, soaps and fragrances.
Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds|Preparatio.explanation: Oxidation of primary alcohols or aldehydes and hydrolysis of nitriles produce acids. Resonance stabilises carboxylate ions. Acids react with bicarbonate releasing CO2, esterify alcohols reversibly, and decarboxylate as sodium salts with soda lime. Electron-withdrawing substituents increase acidity.
Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds|Preparatio.relationship: RCOOH + ROH <=> RCOOR + H2O; RCOONa + NaOH -> RH + Na2CO3
Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds|Preparatio.example: Example: CH3COOH + NaHCO3 -> CH3COONa + CO2 + H2O. CH3COOH + C2H5OH <=> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O with H+ and heat.

Gaseous State: Formative|Boyle Charles G.summary: The empirical gas laws relate pressure, volume, absolute temperature and amount when the other variables are controlled.
Gaseous State: Formative|Boyle Charles G.mistake: Do not answer Boyle Charles Gay-Lussac and Avogadro laws from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion.
Gaseous State: Formative|Boyle Charles G.application: Boyle Charles Gay-Lussac and Avogadro laws supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.
Gaseous State: Formative|Boyle Charles G.explanation: Temperature must be in kelvin, and each law applies only while its stated variables remain constant. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute.
Gaseous State: Formative|Boyle Charles G.relationship: PV constant; V/T constant; P/T constant; V/n constant
Gaseous State: Formative|Boyle Charles G.example: Example: At constant temperature, compressing a gas from 2.0 L to 1.0 L doubles its pressure. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result.

Heat transfer.summary: Heat transfer treats energy transport by conduction, convection and radiation.
Heat transfer.explanation: Treats energy transport by conduction, convection and radiation.
Heat transfer.example: A counter-current heat exchanger uses a log-mean temperature difference to determine required area.

Properties of solids.summary: Solids have a fixed shape and volume and are usually difficult to compress.
Properties of solids.mistake: Particles in a solid are not motionless; they vibrate about fixed positions.
Properties of solids.application: Engineers select solids for buildings, tools and devices by comparing hardness, strength and flexibility.
Properties of solids.explanation: Their particles are packed closely in fixed positions. The particles still vibrate, but strong attractions prevent them from flowing past one another.
Properties of solids.relationship: closely packed particles -> fixed shape and fixed volume
Properties of solids.example: Example: a wooden block keeps its shape when moved from a desk to a box; pressing it does not noticeably reduce its volume.

Mixtures.summary: A mixture contains two or more substances physically combined in variable proportions.
Mixtures.mistake: A homogeneous mixture is not a pure substance even when its components cannot be seen.
Mixtures.application: Separation of mixtures is used in water treatment, food processing, petroleum refining and recycling.
Mixtures.explanation: Each component keeps its identity and can usually be separated using differences in physical properties such as particle size, boiling point or solubility.
Mixtures.relationship: components retain identity; composition can vary
Mixtures.example: Example: salt water can be separated by evaporation or distillation because water is more volatile than salt.

Isoelectronic species.summary: Isoelectronic species have the same total number of electrons.
Isoelectronic species.mistake: Isoelectronic does not mean chemically identical; nuclear charge and element identity still differ.
Isoelectronic species.application: Electron counting helps predict ion sizes, bonding and stable ion formation.
Isoelectronic species.explanation: They may be atoms or ions of different elements. Their sizes can differ because nuclei with more protons attract the shared number of electrons more strongly.
Isoelectronic species.relationship: electrons = atomic number - positive charge + negative charge
Isoelectronic species.example: Example: Ne, Na+ and F- each have 10 electrons and are isoelectronic. This illustrates the key relationship; explain the particles or quantities involved and keep all symbols and units consistent.

Chemical Kinetics|Catalysis.summary: Kinetic catalysis increases reaction rate through an alternative lower-energy mechanism.
Chemical Kinetics|Catalysis.mistake: A catalyst does not increase equilibrium yield or make a thermodynamically impossible process favorable.
Chemical Kinetics|Catalysis.application: Catalysis enables lower-temperature manufacturing, emission control and enzyme-driven life chemistry.
Chemical Kinetics|Catalysis.explanation: A catalyst participates in elementary steps but is regenerated overall. It accelerates forward and reverse processes without changing deltaG, K or equilibrium composition.
Chemical Kinetics|Catalysis.relationship: catalyst -> alternative pathway with lower activation energy
Chemical Kinetics|Catalysis.example: Example: MnO2 accelerates H2O2 decomposition by lowering the pathway barrier and remains chemically regenerated overall.

Nuclear Chemistry|Half-life.summary: Half-life is the time required for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.
Nuclear Chemistry|Half-life.mistake: Half-life does not mean every nucleus decays at that exact time; individual decay is random.
Nuclear Chemistry|Half-life.application: Half-life calculations guide dating, medicine dosing, waste storage and radiation safety.
Nuclear Chemistry|Half-life.explanation: It is constant for a given radionuclide and independent of initial amount. Radioactive decay follows first-order exponential behavior.
Nuclear Chemistry|Half-life.example: Example: after three half-lives, the remaining fraction is (1/2)^3 = 1/8 or 12.5%.

Nuclear Chemistry|Gamma rays.summary: Gamma rays are high-energy photons emitted when an excited nucleus loses energy.
Nuclear Chemistry|Gamma rays.mistake: Gamma rays have no mass or charge, but they are ionizing electromagnetic radiation and can be hazardous.
Nuclear Chemistry|Gamma rays.application: Gamma rays are used in imaging, sterilization, radiotherapy and non-destructive testing.
Nuclear Chemistry|Gamma rays.explanation: Gamma emission changes neither mass number nor atomic number. Gamma radiation penetrates strongly and requires dense shielding.
Nuclear Chemistry|Gamma rays.relationship: excited nucleus -> lower-energy nucleus + gamma photon
Nuclear Chemistry|Gamma rays.example: Example: an excited technetium-99m nucleus emits a gamma photon to reach a lower nuclear energy state without changing element.

Postgraduate|Chemical Engineering Fundam.summary: Reactor design connects kinetics, flow, mixing and heat effects to conversion and selectivity.
Postgraduate|Chemical Engineering Fundam.mistake: Do not treat Reactor design as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Postgraduate|Chemical Engineering Fundam.application: Advanced practitioners use this concept to connect quantitative chemical models with reproducible evidence and practical decisions.
Postgraduate|Chemical Engineering Fundam.explanation: At postgraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Chemical Engineering Fundamentals, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Postgraduate|Chemical Engineering Fundam.relationship: design equation: V = flow x concentration change / rate
Postgraduate|Chemical Engineering Fundam.example: Example: For a first-order reaction, a CSTR and plug-flow reactor require different volumes for the same conversion.

Batteries.summary: Batteries store chemical free energy in coupled electrode reactions and deliver it as electrical work.
Batteries.explanation: Store chemical free energy in coupled electrode reactions and deliver it as electrical work.
Batteries.example: Lithium-ion capacity is estimated from reversible electron transfer per mass of active material.

Nanochemistry.summary: Nanochemistry controls nucleation, growth, surface functionalization and nanoscale property emergence.
Nanochemistry.explanation: Controls nucleation, growth, surface functionalization and nanoscale property emergence.
Nanochemistry.relationship: nucleation rate versus growth rate controls particle size
Nanochemistry.example: A seed-mediated synthesis separates nucleation from growth to narrow a nanoparticle size distribution.

Undergraduate|Advanced Organic Chemistry.summary: Reaction mechanisms describe elementary bond-making and bond-breaking steps consistent with kinetics, stereochemistry and isotope evidence.
Undergraduate|Advanced Organic Chemistry.mistake: Do not treat Reaction mechanisms as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Undergraduate|Advanced Organic Chemistry.application: This reasoning guides selective synthesis of medicines, agrochemicals, probes and functional molecules.
Undergraduate|Advanced Organic Chemistry.explanation: At undergraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Advanced Organic Chemistry, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Undergraduate|Advanced Organic Chemistry.example: Example: An SN2 substitution gives second-order kinetics and inversion at a chiral centre through backside attack.

Gaseous State: Formative|Dalton law of p.summary: For an ideal gas mixture, total pressure is the sum of partial pressures and each partial pressure follows its mole fraction.
Gaseous State: Formative|Dalton law of p.mistake: Do not answer Dalton law of partial pressures from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion.
Gaseous State: Formative|Dalton law of p.application: Dalton law of partial pressures supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.
Gaseous State: Formative|Dalton law of p.explanation: For gas collected over water, subtract water vapour pressure to obtain the dry-gas pressure. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute.
Gaseous State: Formative|Dalton law of p.example: Example: In a mixture with xO2=0.21 at 100 kPa total pressure, pO2=21 kPa. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result.

Discovery of atom.summary: The atomic idea developed from philosophical proposals into an evidence-based scientific model.
Discovery of atom.mistake: No single scientist discovered the complete modern atom at once.
Discovery of atom.application: Atomic models explain materials, electricity, spectra, medicines and nuclear energy.
Discovery of atom.explanation: Democritus suggested indivisible particles, but later experiments by Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr and others revealed atoms, electrons, nuclei and quantized behavior.
Discovery of atom.example: Example: cathode-ray experiments showed that all atoms contain the same negatively charged particle, the electron.

Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.summary: State symbols and observation notes connect a symbolic equation with what is actually seen during a reaction.
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.mistake: Do not write (aq) for every liquid: aqueous means dissolved in water, while pure liquid water is marked (l).
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.application: Clear observation records help identify substances, verify reactions and communicate laboratory results safely.
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.explanation: Use (s), (l), (g) and (aq) for solid, liquid, gas and aqueous solution. Record evidence such as colour change, gas evolution, precipitate formation, temperature change, light or odour without confusing observation with particle-level inference.
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.relationship: CaCO3(s) --heat--> CaO(s) + CO2(g); AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) -> AgCl(s)↓ + NaNO3(aq)
Class 10 Chemical Substances and Carbon|.example: Example: Mixing colourless silver-nitrate and sodium-chloride solutions produces a white precipitate. 'White solid appears' is the observation; 'AgCl formed' is the chemical inference.

Undergraduate|Spectroscopy|XRD.summary: XRD X-ray diffraction determines long-range crystal structure from constructive interference by lattice planes.
Undergraduate|Spectroscopy|XRD.mistake: Do not treat XRD as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Undergraduate|Spectroscopy|XRD.application: Laboratories use this method for defensible identification, quantification, purity testing and structure determination.
Undergraduate|Spectroscopy|XRD.explanation: At undergraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Spectroscopy, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Undergraduate|Spectroscopy|XRD.example: Example: A peak at known wavelength and angle gives interplanar spacing through Bragg's law.

Ideal gas equation.summary: The ideal gas equation combines pressure, volume, amount and absolute temperature.
Ideal gas equation.mistake: Choose an R value consistent with the pressure and volume units, and always use kelvin.
Ideal gas equation.application: The equation estimates gas amounts, molar masses, densities and process conditions.
Ideal gas equation.explanation: PV = nRT models particles with negligible volume and no intermolecular attractions. Real gases approach ideal behavior at low pressure and high temperature.
Ideal gas equation.example: Example: one mole of ideal gas at 273.15 K and 1 atm occupies about 22.4 L using R = 0.08206 L atm mol-1 K-1.

Postgraduate|Astrochemistry|Core princip.summary: Astrochemistry studies molecule formation and spectroscopy in interstellar, circumstellar and planetary environments.
Postgraduate|Astrochemistry|Core princip.mistake: Do not treat Core principles and applications as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Postgraduate|Astrochemistry|Core princip.application: Advanced practitioners use this concept to connect quantitative chemical models with reproducible evidence and practical decisions.
Postgraduate|Astrochemistry|Core princip.explanation: At postgraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Astrochemistry, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Postgraduate|Astrochemistry|Core princip.example: Example: Rotational lines identify molecules in a cold cloud by matching multiple transitions at one velocity.

Scientific writing.summary: Scientific writing communicates methods, evidence, uncertainty and interpretation in a reproducible scholarly form.
Scientific writing.explanation: Communicates methods, evidence, uncertainty and interpretation in a reproducible scholarly form.
Scientific writing.example: A results section reports calibrated values and uncertainty, while discussion separates observation from mechanistic inference.

Food Chemistry.summary: Food Chemistry studies molecular composition, processing reactions, texture, flavour, nutrition and safety.
Food Chemistry.explanation: Studies molecular composition, processing reactions, texture, flavour, nutrition and safety.
Food Chemistry.relationship: composition + processing -> structure, flavour and stability
Food Chemistry.example: Maillard browning between reducing sugars and amino groups creates colour and aroma during heating.

Thermochemistry|Born-Haber cycle.summary: A Born-Haber cycle applies Hess Law to ionic-solid formation.
Thermochemistry|Born-Haber cycle.mistake: Track stoichiometric factors and signs carefully, especially half a diatomic bond and the electron-affinity convention.
Thermochemistry|Born-Haber cycle.application: Born-Haber cycles compare ionic stability, lattice energy and plausibility of oxidation states.
Thermochemistry|Born-Haber cycle.explanation: It combines atomization, ionization, electron affinity, bond dissociation and lattice steps so an unmeasurable lattice enthalpy can be inferred.
Thermochemistry|Born-Haber cycle.relationship: deltaHformation = sum of atom and ion steps + lattice enthalpy
Thermochemistry|Born-Haber cycle.example: Example: a NaCl cycle links sodium sublimation, chlorine bond dissociation, sodium ionization, chlorine electron gain and NaCl lattice formation.

Thomson model.summary: Thomson's model pictured negative electrons embedded in a diffuse positively charged atom.
Thomson model.mistake: Do not place a nucleus in Thomson's model; the nucleus was introduced after Rutherford's evidence.
Thomson model.application: The model shows how scientific explanations change when new particles are discovered.
Thomson model.explanation: It was proposed after the electron was discovered and explained overall electrical neutrality, but it had no central nucleus.
Thomson model.relationship: total positive charge + total negative charge = neutral atom
Thomson model.example: Example: the model is often compared to raisins distributed through a pudding, with electrons spread inside positive matter.

Undergraduate|Biochemistry|Proteins.summary: Proteins are amino-acid polymers whose sequence drives folding, dynamics and biological function.
Undergraduate|Biochemistry|Proteins.mistake: Do not treat Proteins as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Undergraduate|Biochemistry|Proteins.application: This concept links molecular structure and chemical reactivity with measurable biological function.
Undergraduate|Biochemistry|Proteins.explanation: At undergraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Biochemistry, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Undergraduate|Biochemistry|Proteins.example: Example: Replacing a buried hydrophobic residue with a charged residue can destabilize a protein core and reduce activity.

Pure substances.summary: A pure substance contains one kind of element or compound and has a fixed composition.
Pure substances.mistake: In everyday speech 'pure' can mean clean, but in chemistry it means one substance with fixed composition.
Pure substances.application: Purity standards protect medicines, food, drinking water and laboratory results.
Pure substances.explanation: It has characteristic properties such as a definite melting point at a stated pressure. Physical methods cannot separate an element or compound into mixture components.
Pure substances.example: Example: pure sodium chloride always contains sodium and chlorine in a fixed 1:1 ion ratio.

Isotones.summary: Isotones are atoms of different elements with the same number of neutrons.
Isotones.mistake: Equal mass number does not make isotones; equal neutron number does.
Isotones.application: Isotones help scientists compare nuclear stability across different elements.
Isotones.explanation: Their atomic and mass numbers differ, but N = A - Z gives the same result.
Isotones.relationship: same N, where N = A - Z
Isotones.example: Example: carbon-14 has 8 neutrons and nitrogen-15 also has 8, so they are isotones.

Undergraduate|Industrial Chemistry|Explo.summary: Explosives release hot gases extremely rapidly through strongly exothermic decomposition or redox chemistry.
Undergraduate|Industrial Chemistry|Explo.mistake: Do not treat Explosives as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Undergraduate|Industrial Chemistry|Explo.application: Industrial chemists balance conversion, selectivity, safety, energy use, quality and environmental impact.
Undergraduate|Industrial Chemistry|Explo.explanation: At undergraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Industrial Chemistry, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Undergraduate|Industrial Chemistry|Explo.relationship: rapid gas generation + heat -> pressure wave
Undergraduate|Industrial Chemistry|Explo.example: Example: An oxygen-balance calculation assesses whether an energetic formulation can oxidize its carbon and hydrogen internally.

Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.summary: The physical and chemical properties of elements are periodic functions of atomic number.
Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.mistake: Do not answer Modern periodic law and long-form table from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion.
Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.application: Modern periodic law and long-form table supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.
Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.explanation: The long-form table has seven periods and eighteen groups; position follows valence-shell electronic configuration. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute.
Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.relationship: period number = highest occupied n; block = differentiating subshell
Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.example: Example: [Ne]3s2 places magnesium in period 3, s-block and group 2. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result.

ESR.summary: ESR electron spin resonance detects species with unpaired electrons and reports their electronic environment.
ESR.explanation: Electron spin resonance detects species with unpaired electrons and reports their electronic environment.
ESR.example: A radical interacting with one proton can show a two-line hyperfine pattern when equivalent-state assumptions apply.

Moles.summary: The mole is the SI unit for amount of substance.
Moles.mistake: Do not use grams directly as equation coefficients; balanced equations compare amounts in moles.
Moles.application: Moles allow chemists to scale reactions, formulations and material compositions.
Moles.explanation: One mole contains Avogadro's number of specified entities. Molar mass converts between amount in moles and measured mass.
Moles.example: Example: 18.0 g of water divided by its molar mass, 18.0 g/mol, equals 1.00 mol H2O.

Bioorganic Chemistry.summary: Bioorganic Chemistry applies organic mechanism and synthesis to biomolecules and biological transformations.
Bioorganic Chemistry.explanation: Applies organic mechanism and synthesis to biomolecules and biological transformations.
Bioorganic Chemistry.example: A mechanism-based inhibitor forms a reactive intermediate only after enzyme processing, producing selective inhibition.

Avogadro number.summary: Avogadro's number is the number of specified particles in one mole: exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
Avogadro number.mistake: Always state the entity being counted; one mole of O atoms differs from one mole of O2 molecules.
Avogadro number.application: The constant connects measured masses with particle counts in reactions and materials.
Avogadro number.explanation: It links the microscopic count of atoms, molecules or ions to laboratory-scale amounts.
Avogadro number.relationship: number of particles = moles × Avogadro constant
Avogadro number.example: Example: 0.50 mol of oxygen molecules contains 0.50 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 3.011 × 10²³ O₂ molecules.

Antibiotics.summary: Antibiotics selectively inhibit bacterial processes while requiring resistance-aware dosing and stewardship.
Antibiotics.explanation: Selectively inhibit bacterial processes while requiring resistance-aware dosing and stewardship.
Antibiotics.relationship: exposure relative to MIC helps predict antibacterial effect
Antibiotics.example: Beta-lactams inhibit cell-wall transpeptidases, but beta-lactamase production can destroy the drug.

Undergraduate|Advanced Organic Chemistry.summary: Rearrangements move atoms or groups within a reactive intermediate to form a more stable skeleton or electron arrangement.
Undergraduate|Advanced Organic Chemistry.mistake: Do not treat Rearrangements as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Undergraduate|Advanced Organic Chemistry.application: This reasoning guides selective synthesis of medicines, agrochemicals, probes and functional molecules.
Undergraduate|Advanced Organic Chemistry.explanation: At undergraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Advanced Organic Chemistry, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Undergraduate|Advanced Organic Chemistry.relationship: migrating group moves with its bonding electron pair
Undergraduate|Advanced Organic Chemistry.example: Example: A Wagner-Meerwein 1,2-shift can convert a less stable carbocation into a more substituted cation before capture.

Mass number.summary: Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in one atom's nucleus.
Mass number.mistake: Mass number for one isotope is not the same as the decimal relative atomic mass on a periodic table.
Mass number.application: Mass number helps identify isotopes and calculate neutron numbers.
Mass number.explanation: It is a whole number written A. Electrons contribute so little mass that they are not counted in the mass number.
Mass number.example: Example: sodium-23 has 11 protons and 12 neutrons, so A = 11 + 12 = 23. This illustrates the key relationship; explain the particles or quantities involved and keep all symbols and units consistent.

Postgraduate|Catalysis|Photocatalysis.summary: Photocatalysis uses absorbed light to generate reactive excited states or electron-hole pairs that drive chemistry.
Postgraduate|Catalysis|Photocatalysis.mistake: Do not treat Photocatalysis as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.

Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.example: Example: Boron has lower first ionization enthalpy than beryllium because a 2p electron is removed more easily than a filled 2s electron. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result.

Microfluidics.summary: Microfluidics controls microlitre-to-picolitre fluids in channels where laminar flow and diffusion dominate.
Microfluidics.explanation: Controls microlitre-to-picolitre fluids in channels where laminar flow and diffusion dominate.
Microfluidics.relationship: Reynolds number is typically low; mixing is diffusion-controlled
Microfluidics.example: Droplet microfluidics creates uniform nanolitre reactors for high-throughput screening.

Bioinorganic Chemistry.summary: Bioinorganic Chemistry examines metal-ion homeostasis, metalloenzymes, electron transfer and metal-based therapeutics.
Bioinorganic Chemistry.explanation: Examines metal-ion homeostasis, metalloenzymes, electron transfer and metal-based therapeutics.
Bioinorganic Chemistry.relationship: metal coordination tunes acidity and redox potential
Bioinorganic Chemistry.example: Zinc in carbonic anhydrase activates bound water for rapid CO2 hydration.

Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds|Preparatio.summary: Ethers are prepared by dehydration of alcohols or Williamson synthesis and generally react only under strong cleavage conditions.
Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds|Preparatio.mistake: Do not choose a tertiary haloalkane for Williamson synthesis or predict cleavage of the aryl C-O bond in anisole under ordinary HI treatment.
Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds|Preparatio.application: Ethers are solvents, anaesthetic-related compounds, fuel additives and intermediates in organic synthesis.
Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds|Preparatio.explanation: Williamson synthesis is an SN2 reaction between an alkoxide and a primary alkyl halide; tertiary halides tend to eliminate. Symmetrical ethers can form by intermolecular dehydration of primary alcohols near 413 K. Hot concentrated HI or HBr cleaves C-O bonds, with aryl-alkyl ethers cleaving on the alkyl side.
Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds|Preparatio.relationship: RONa + R'X -> ROR' + NaX; ROR' + HI -> RI + R'OH
Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds|Preparatio.example: Example: C2H5ONa + CH3I -> C2H5OCH3 + NaI. Anisole + HI gives phenol and CH3I rather than iodobenzene.

p-Block Elements: Formative|Oxidation st.summary: p-Block elements show variable oxidation states; the lower state becomes more stable down heavier groups as the ns2 pair becomes less available for bonding.
p-Block Elements: Formative|Oxidation st.mistake: Do not answer Oxidation states and inert-pair effect from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion.
p-Block Elements: Formative|Oxidation st.application: Oxidation states and inert-pair effect supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.
p-Block Elements: Formative|Oxidation st.explanation: The inert-pair effect is a stability trend, not a claim that the s electrons can never participate in bonding. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute.
p-Block Elements: Formative|Oxidation st.relationship: group 14: +4 and +2; group 15: +5 and +3; lower state stabilises down group
p-Block Elements: Formative|Oxidation st.example: Example: Pb(II) is more stable than Pb(IV), whereas C(IV) is the dominant carbon oxidation state. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result.

Homogeneous.summary: Homogeneous catalysis uses catalyst and reactants in one phase, enabling molecularly defined active sites and tunable ligands.
Homogeneous.explanation: Catalysis uses catalyst and reactants in one phase, enabling molecularly defined active sites and tunable ligands.
Homogeneous.relationship: rate and selectivity depend on catalyst speciation
Homogeneous.example: A soluble rhodium complex catalyses alkene hydrogenation through oxidative addition, coordination and reductive elimination.

Gaseous State: Formative|Real gases and.summary: Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour when intermolecular attractions and molecular volume become significant.
Gaseous State: Formative|Real gases and.mistake: Do not answer Real gases and compressibility factor from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion.
Gaseous State: Formative|Real gases and.application: Real gases and compressibility factor supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.
Gaseous State: Formative|Real gases and.explanation: Deviation is strongest at high pressure and low temperature, not a fixed property independent of conditions. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute.
Gaseous State: Formative|Real gases and.example: Example: A gas with Z below one shows attraction-dominated negative deviation; Z above one indicates repulsion or excluded-volume dominance. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result.

VSEPR.summary: VSEPR theory predicts shape by arranging electron domains to minimize repulsion around a central atom.
VSEPR.mistake: Do not count a double bond as two domains or include lone pairs as atoms in the molecular-shape name.
VSEPR.application: VSEPR predicts shapes that control polarity, biological binding and material behavior.
VSEPR.explanation: Bonding pairs and lone pairs count as domains; lone pairs repel more strongly and can compress bond angles.
VSEPR.example: Example: NH3 has four electron domains but one lone pair, giving tetrahedral electron geometry and trigonal-pyramidal molecular shape.

Surface Chemistry|Catalysis.summary: Surface catalysis occurs when reactants adsorb and react at active sites on a catalyst.
Surface Chemistry|Catalysis.mistake: A catalyst surface is not uniformly active; defects, facets and poisons strongly affect performance.
Surface Chemistry|Catalysis.application: Heterogeneous catalysis enables fertilizers, fuels, pollution control and many bulk chemicals.
Surface Chemistry|Catalysis.explanation: Adsorption brings molecules together and weakens bonds; products then desorb, freeing sites. Excessively strong adsorption can poison or block the surface.
Surface Chemistry|Catalysis.example: Example: finely divided iron provides surface sites for nitrogen and hydrogen during ammonia synthesis.

Smart materials.summary: Smart materials respond predictably to stimuli such as temperature, light, pH, stress or electric field.
Smart materials.explanation: Respond predictably to stimuli such as temperature, light, pH, stress or electric field.
Smart materials.relationship: stimulus -> reversible structural response -> property change
Smart materials.example: A shape-memory alloy returns to a programmed shape when heating triggers a reversible phase transformation.

Aufbau.summary: The Aufbau principle states that electrons occupy lower-energy orbitals before higher-energy orbitals.
Aufbau.mistake: Do not treat the diagonal filling order as exception-free, especially for chromium and copper.
Aufbau.application: Aufbau filling helps construct ground-state configurations and understand periodic organization.
Aufbau.explanation: The usual filling order follows increasing n + l; when two subshells have equal n + l, the one with lower n fills first. Some transition elements have exceptions.
Aufbau.relationship: lower orbital energy fills first; use the n + l rule
Aufbau.example: Example: potassium fills 4s before 3d, giving [Ar]4s1 because 4s is lower in energy for the neutral atom at that stage.

Vapour pressure.summary: Vapour pressure is the pressure of vapour in dynamic equilibrium with its liquid at a given temperature.
Vapour pressure.mistake: Vapour pressure is not the same as atmospheric pressure and applies even below the boiling point.
Vapour pressure.application: Vapour pressure informs distillation, fuel storage, drying and solvent safety.
Vapour pressure.explanation: Faster molecules escape the surface while vapour molecules condense. Higher temperature raises vapour pressure; stronger attractions lower it.
Vapour pressure.relationship: boiling occurs when vapour pressure = external pressure
Vapour pressure.example: Example: a liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals external pressure, so water boils below 100 degrees C at high altitude.

Postgraduate|Advanced Laboratory Techniq.summary: Schlenk line combines vacuum and inert-gas manifolds for controlled evacuation, backfilling and transfer.
Postgraduate|Advanced Laboratory Techniq.mistake: Do not treat Schlenk line as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Postgraduate|Advanced Laboratory Techniq.application: Researchers use this practice to obtain reproducible, traceable and uncertainty-aware experimental evidence.
Postgraduate|Advanced Laboratory Techniq.explanation: At postgraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Advanced Laboratory Techniques, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Postgraduate|Advanced Laboratory Techniq.example: Example: A flask is cycled vacuum/inert gas before reagent addition and maintained under positive inert pressure.

Accuracy.summary: Accuracy describes how close a measurement is to the accepted or true value.
Accuracy.mistake: One measurement can be accurate by chance; repeated measurements are needed to judge a method.
Accuracy.application: Accurate measurements protect medicine doses, product quality and environmental limits.
Accuracy.explanation: Accuracy depends on correct calibration, procedure and freedom from systematic bias.
Accuracy.relationship: smaller difference from accepted value -> greater accuracy
Accuracy.example: Example: if a reference mass is 10.00 g, a reading of 10.01 g is more accurate than 9.70 g.

Postgraduate|Advanced Laboratory Techniq.summary: Cryogenic techniques use very low temperatures to control reactivity, trap intermediates or study phase and quantum behaviour.
Postgraduate|Advanced Laboratory Techniq.mistake: Do not treat Cryogenic techniques as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Postgraduate|Advanced Laboratory Techniq.application: Researchers use this practice to obtain reproducible, traceable and uncertainty-aware experimental evidence.
Postgraduate|Advanced Laboratory Techniq.explanation: At postgraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Advanced Laboratory Techniques, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Postgraduate|Advanced Laboratory Techniq.relationship: cooling changes rate constants and phase equilibria
Postgraduate|Advanced Laboratory Techniq.example: Example: A reaction at -78 C slows side pathways while controlled warming completes conversion.

Synthetic Organic Chemistry.summary: Synthetic Organic Chemistry plans and executes selective multistep construction using mechanism, chemoselectivity and protecting-group strategy.
Synthetic Organic Chemistry.explanation: Plans and executes selective multistep construction using mechanism, chemoselectivity and protecting-group strategy.
Synthetic Organic Chemistry.relationship: overall yield = product of fractional step yields
Synthetic Organic Chemistry.example: A convergent route couples two advanced fragments and can outperform a long linear sequence.

Organic Purification and Analysis|Chroma.summary: Chromatography separates substances by different interactions with stationary and mobile phases.
Organic Purification and Analysis|Chroma.mistake: Do not answer Chromatographic purification from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion.
Organic Purification and Analysis|Chroma.application: Chromatographic purification supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.
Organic Purification and Analysis|Chroma.explanation: Mark the origin in pencil, keep it above solvent and compare Rf only under identical conditions. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute.
Organic Purification and Analysis|Chroma.relationship: Rf = distance travelled by solute / distance travelled by solvent front
Organic Purification and Analysis|Chroma.example: Example: Paper chromatography separates ink dyes; an Rf of 3.0/5.0 = 0.60 under the stated conditions. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result.

Undergraduate|Separation Techniques|Ion.summary: Ion exchange separates ions through reversible electrostatic binding to charged resin sites.
Undergraduate|Separation Techniques|Ion.mistake: Do not treat Ion exchange as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Undergraduate|Separation Techniques|Ion.application: Laboratories use this method for defensible identification, quantification, purity testing and structure determination.
Undergraduate|Separation Techniques|Ion.explanation: At undergraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Separation Techniques, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Undergraduate|Separation Techniques|Ion.example: Example: A cation-exchange resin retains Ca2+ more strongly than Na+ under suitable conditions because charge and selectivity differ.

pH.summary: pH is a logarithmic measure related to hydronium-ion concentration.
pH.mistake: pH 3 is ten times more acidic by hydronium concentration than pH 4, not merely one unit more.
pH.application: pH control is vital in blood, soil, food, medicines, pools and wastewater.
pH.explanation: At school level, pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is basic for water near room temperature. Each pH unit represents a tenfold concentration change.
pH.example: Example: if [H3O+] = 1.0 x 10^-3 mol/L, pH = -log(1.0 x 10^-3) = 3.00. Identify the given quantities or particles, apply the relationship, and check units and chemical meaning.

Undergraduate|Polymer Chemistry|Biopolym.summary: Biopolymers are natural or bio-derived macromolecules whose sequence and interactions control biological or material function.
Undergraduate|Polymer Chemistry|Biopolym.mistake: Do not treat Biopolymers as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Undergraduate|Polymer Chemistry|Biopolym.application: This concept connects processing and molecular structure with useful mechanical, electrical, optical or biological performance.
Undergraduate|Polymer Chemistry|Biopolym.explanation: At undergraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Polymer Chemistry, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Undergraduate|Polymer Chemistry|Biopolym.example: Example: Cellulose contains beta-linked glucose chains whose hydrogen-bonded assembly gives strong fibres.

Oxidation.summary: Oxidation is loss of electrons; at an introductory level it can also be recognized as gain of oxygen.
Oxidation.mistake: Oxidation does not always involve oxygen. Check the definition, particles and evidence before deciding.
Oxidation.application: Oxidation occurs in combustion, rusting, respiration, bleaching and batteries.
Oxidation.explanation: Oxidation and reduction happen together because electrons lost by one species must be gained by another.
Oxidation.example: Example: Mg -> Mg2+ + 2e- shows magnesium being oxidized during formation of magnesium oxide.

Subatomic particles.summary: Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons.
Subatomic particles.mistake: Do not say neutrons have no mass; they have no electrical charge.
Subatomic particles.application: Subatomic particles explain ions, isotopes, electricity and nuclear reactions.
Subatomic particles.explanation: Protons have charge +1 and neutrons have charge 0 in the nucleus; electrons have charge -1 and occupy the surrounding electron cloud. Protons and neutrons are much more massive than electrons.
Subatomic particles.example: Example: a neutral carbon-12 atom has 6 protons, 6 neutrons and 6 electrons. This illustrates the key relationship; explain the particles or quantities involved and keep all symbols and units consistent.

Modern atomic model.summary: The modern atomic model describes electrons with probability regions called orbitals.
Modern atomic model.mistake: An orbital is not a solid shell or a track followed by an electron.
Modern atomic model.application: The modern model predicts bonding, spectra, semiconductor behavior and chemical reactivity.
Modern atomic model.explanation: Quantum mechanics does not assign an electron a fixed circular path. Orbitals show where an electron is likely to be found and have quantized energies and shapes.
Modern atomic model.relationship: orbital = region of high probability of finding an electron
Modern atomic model.example: Example: the lowest-energy electron in hydrogen occupies a spherical 1s orbital, represented as a probability cloud.

Isotopes.summary: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different neutron numbers.
Isotopes.mistake: Isotopes are not different elements because their atomic numbers are the same.
Isotopes.application: Isotopes are used in medical imaging, cancer treatment, dating and chemical tracing.
Isotopes.explanation: They have similar chemical behavior because they have the same electron arrangement, but their masses and nuclear stability can differ.
Isotopes.example: Example: carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have 6 protons; they have 6 and 8 neutrons respectively.

Electrochemistry|Nernst equation.summary: The Nernst equation gives electrode or cell potential under nonstandard conditions.
Electrochemistry|Nernst equation.mistake: Construct Q from the balanced cell reaction and omit pure solids and liquids.
Electrochemistry|Nernst equation.application: The Nernst equation supports concentration sensors, batteries, pH electrodes and equilibrium calculations.
Electrochemistry|Nernst equation.explanation: Potential depends logarithmically on reaction quotient and approaches zero at equilibrium for the full cell. Temperature and electron count must be specified.
Electrochemistry|Nernst equation.example: Example: at 298 K, E = Estandard - (0.05916/n)log Q; increasing product activity lowers E for the written cell reaction.

Electrochemistry|EMF.summary: Electromotive force is the maximum potential difference of a cell when essentially no current flows.
Electrochemistry|EMF.mistake: EMF is a voltage, not a mechanical force, and standard potentials are not multiplied by stoichiometric coefficients.
Electrochemistry|EMF.application: EMF determines battery voltage, sensor response and available electrical work.
Electrochemistry|EMF.explanation: Positive Ecell for the written reaction indicates a spontaneous galvanic process under those conditions and connects directly with Gibbs free energy.
Electrochemistry|EMF.example: Example: if Ecathode = +0.34 V and Eanode reduction potential = -0.76 V, Ecell = 0.34 - (-0.76) = 1.10 V.

Class 9 Matter and Mixtures|Paper chroma.summary: Paper chromatography separates dissolved substances because they travel differently with a solvent over paper.
Class 9 Matter and Mixtures|Paper chroma.mistake: Do not draw the baseline in ink or immerse the sample spot in solvent; either action contaminates or washes away the starting sample.
Class 9 Matter and Mixtures|Paper chroma.application: Chromatography separates inks, food colours, plant pigments and components used in forensic or quality-control comparisons.
Class 9 Matter and Mixtures|Paper chroma.explanation: Place a small sample spot on a pencil baseline above the solvent. The solvent rises by capillary action; components repeatedly partition between the mobile solvent and stationary water/paper environment. Mark the solvent front immediately and compare spots using Rf under identical conditions.
Class 9 Matter and Mixtures|Paper chroma.relationship: Rf = distance travelled by solute / distance travelled by solvent front; 0 <= Rf <= 1
Class 9 Matter and Mixtures|Paper chroma.example: Example: If an ink dye travels 3.0 cm while the solvent front travels 5.0 cm, Rf = 3.0/5.0 = 0.60.

Solar cells.summary: Solar cells convert absorbed photons into separated charge carriers and electrical power.
Solar cells.explanation: Convert absorbed photons into separated charge carriers and electrical power.
Solar cells.relationship: efficiency = electrical power out / solar power in
Solar cells.example: A semiconductor junction creates a built-in field that separates photogenerated electron-hole pairs.

Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.summary: The Kossel-Lewis approach explains bond formation through valence electrons, noble-gas configurations and shared or transferred electron pairs.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.mistake: Do not answer Kossel-Lewis approach from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.application: Kossel-Lewis approach supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.explanation: Lewis symbols track valence electrons and distinguish electrovalent attraction from directional covalent bonding. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.relationship: ionic: electron transfer; covalent: shared electron pair
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure.example: Example: Sodium transfers one electron to chlorine to form Na+ and Cl-, whereas two chlorine atoms share a pair in Cl2. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result.

Polymerization.summary: Polymerization joins monomers into macromolecules by chain-growth or step-growth pathways.
Polymerization.explanation: Joins monomers into macromolecules by chain-growth or step-growth pathways.
Polymerization.relationship: degree of polymerization = polymer molar mass / repeat-unit molar mass
Polymerization.example: Free-radical ethene polymerization uses initiation, propagation and termination to form polyethylene.

Hund rule.summary: Hund's rule states that electrons occupy equal-energy orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing.
Hund rule.mistake: Do not pair electrons in one p orbital while another orbital of the same subshell is empty.
Hund rule.application: Hund's rule predicts unpaired electrons and therefore helps explain magnetic behavior.
Hund rule.explanation: Spreading electrons across degenerate orbitals reduces repulsion and gives a lower-energy arrangement.
Hund rule.relationship: degenerate orbitals: single occupation before pairing
Hund rule.example: Example: nitrogen's three 2p electrons occupy the three p orbitals separately with parallel spins rather than pairing in one orbital.

School Practical Chemistry|Representing.summary: Well-designed tables and graphs reveal patterns while preserving units, uncertainty and the distinction between measured and calculated values.
School Practical Chemistry|Representing.mistake: Do not omit units, force a graph through the origin without scientific reason or delete an anomalous result merely to improve the trend.
School Practical Chemistry|Representing.application: Accurate data representation supports solubility analysis, reaction comparisons, calibration and clear scientific communication.
School Practical Chemistry|Representing.explanation: Place the independent variable in the first table column and on the horizontal graph axis; place the dependent variable on the vertical axis. Use headings with units, sensible scales, plotted points and a best-fit line or curve rather than joining automatically. Report anomalous points honestly and calculate averages only when appropriate.
School Practical Chemistry|Representing.relationship: graph: x = independent variable; y = dependent variable; gradient = change in y/change in x
School Practical Chemistry|Representing.example: Example: For solubility versus temperature, tabulate temperature in °C and solubility in g per 100 g water, plot points and draw a smooth curve to estimate intermediate values.

Undergraduate|Advanced Physical Chemistr.summary: Spectroscopy infers structure and dynamics from the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with quantized molecular states.
Undergraduate|Advanced Physical Chemistr.mistake: Do not treat Spectroscopy as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Undergraduate|Advanced Physical Chemistr.application: These models predict molecular energies, equilibrium, phases and non-ideal behaviour in research and process design.
Undergraduate|Advanced Physical Chemistr.explanation: At undergraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Advanced Physical Chemistry, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Undergraduate|Advanced Physical Chemistr.example: Example: An IR absorption at about 1700 cm-1 is evidence for many carbonyl groups, but the full spectrum must confirm identity.

Undergraduate|Medicinal Chemistry|SAR.summary: SAR structure-activity relationships connect controlled molecular changes with measured biological effects.
Undergraduate|Medicinal Chemistry|SAR.mistake: Do not treat SAR as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Undergraduate|Medicinal Chemistry|SAR.application: Drug teams apply this evidence to optimize efficacy, exposure, formulation, stability and safety.
Undergraduate|Medicinal Chemistry|SAR.explanation: At undergraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Medicinal Chemistry, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Undergraduate|Medicinal Chemistry|SAR.relationship: structural change -> property change -> activity change
Undergraduate|Medicinal Chemistry|SAR.example: Example: Replacing a methyl group with chlorine may improve potency but must also be checked for lipophilicity and clearance changes.

Thermochemistry|Specific heat.summary: Specific heat capacity is the heat required to raise one unit mass of a substance by one kelvin.
Thermochemistry|Specific heat.mistake: Use the mass of the material being heated and keep heat-capacity units consistent with mass units.
Thermochemistry|Specific heat.application: Specific heat guides cooling systems, cooking, climate models and material selection.
Thermochemistry|Specific heat.explanation: It is an intensive material property over a stated temperature range. Water's high value makes it an effective thermal buffer.
Thermochemistry|Specific heat.example: Example: heating 100 g water by 5.0 K requires q = 100 x 4.18 x 5.0 = 2.09 kJ. State the sign convention, substitute consistent units, and interpret the numerical result chemically.

Undergraduate|Environmental Chemistry|Wa.summary: Water pollution covers chemical, biological and physical contamination that degrades water quality and ecosystems.
Undergraduate|Environmental Chemistry|Wa.mistake: Do not treat Water pollution as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Undergraduate|Environmental Chemistry|Wa.application: This chemistry supports monitoring, source attribution, risk assessment and evidence-based environmental control.
Undergraduate|Environmental Chemistry|Wa.explanation: At undergraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Environmental Chemistry, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Undergraduate|Environmental Chemistry|Wa.example: Example: Excess phosphate drives algal growth; decomposition then consumes dissolved oxygen and can cause fish death.

Temperature scales.summary: Temperature measures how hot or cold a system is and is reported using scales such as Celsius and kelvin.
Temperature scales.mistake: A temperature of 0 degrees C is not zero particle motion; 0 K is absolute zero.
Temperature scales.application: Temperature control is essential in food storage, reactions, medicine and weather observations.
Temperature scales.explanation: Celsius sets water's freezing point near 0 degrees C at standard pressure. Kelvin begins at absolute zero and has no negative values.
Temperature scales.example: Example: 25 degrees C = 25 + 273.15 = 298.15 K. This illustrates the key relationship; explain the particles or quantities involved and keep all symbols and units consistent.

Covalent bond.summary: A covalent bond forms when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
Covalent bond.mistake: Sharing is not always perfectly equal; electronegativity differences can make a covalent bond polar.
Covalent bond.application: Covalent bonding creates molecules, polymers, biomolecules and network solids.
Covalent bond.explanation: Shared electron density attracts both nuclei. Single, double and triple bonds differ in shared pairs, length and strength.
Covalent bond.example: Example: in H2, each hydrogen contributes one electron to a shared pair, allowing both atoms to achieve a stable duet.

Lewis structures.summary: Lewis structures show valence electrons as bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Lewis structures.mistake: Do not add or remove electrons without accounting for the overall charge of the species.
Lewis structures.application: Lewis structures help predict bonding, resonance, geometry, polarity and reactivity.
Lewis structures.explanation: A reliable structure counts all valence electrons, connects atoms, completes outer shells where possible and checks formal charges.
Lewis structures.relationship: formal charge = valence electrons - lone electrons - number of bonds
Lewis structures.example: Example: CO2 is drawn O=C=O with two lone pairs on each oxygen; all atoms reach octets and formal charges are zero.

Physical changes.summary: A physical change alters form, size or state without producing a new substance.
Physical changes.mistake: Reversibility alone is not a perfect test; focus on whether a new substance forms.
Physical changes.application: Physical changes are used in cutting, grinding, melting, freezing and separating mixtures.
Physical changes.explanation: The particles keep their chemical identity, although their spacing, arrangement or motion may change. Many physical changes are reversible.
Physical changes.example: Example: melting ice changes solid H2O to liquid H2O; cooling can reverse the change.

Chemical Equilibrium|Ionic equilibrium.summary: Ionic equilibrium describes reversible ionization and ion reactions in solution.
Chemical Equilibrium|Ionic equilibrium.mistake: Do not treat weak electrolytes as fully dissociated or ignore charge and mass balance.
Chemical Equilibrium|Ionic equilibrium.application: Ionic equilibria determine pH, precipitation, water chemistry and analytical separations.
Chemical Equilibrium|Ionic equilibrium.explanation: Weak acids, weak bases, water and sparingly soluble salts establish equilibria described by Ka, Kb, Kw and Ksp.
Chemical Equilibrium|Ionic equilibrium.example: Example: for HA <-> H+ + A-, Ka = [H+][A-]/[HA]; a smaller Ka indicates less ionization under comparable conditions.

Volumetric analysis.summary: Volumetric analysis determines analyte amount from the accurately measured volume of a standardized reagent.
Volumetric analysis.explanation: Determines analyte amount from the accurately measured volume of a standardized reagent.
Volumetric analysis.relationship: moles titrant / coefficient = moles analyte / coefficient
Volumetric analysis.example: At equivalence, 25.00 mL of 0.1000 M HCl requires 25.00 mL of 0.1000 M NaOH.

Undergraduate|Industrial Chemistry|Petro.summary: Petrochemicals are industrial chemicals derived mainly from petroleum or natural-gas feedstocks.
Undergraduate|Industrial Chemistry|Petro.mistake: Do not treat Petrochemicals as a label or a result from one instrument alone. Check calibration or model assumptions, chemical plausibility, uncertainty and independent evidence.
Undergraduate|Industrial Chemistry|Petro.application: Industrial chemists balance conversion, selectivity, safety, energy use, quality and environmental impact.
Undergraduate|Industrial Chemistry|Petro.explanation: At undergraduate level, use the stated model quantitatively, identify its assumptions and connect every prediction with experimental or computational evidence. For Industrial Chemistry, compare plausible alternatives, preserve units and chemical constraints, and report uncertainty or limitations before accepting a conclusion.
Undergraduate|Industrial Chemistry|Petro.example: Example: Steam cracking converts larger hydrocarbons into ethene and propene used for polymers and intermediates.

Molecular dynamics.summary: Molecular dynamics propagates atomic motion over time using forces from a potential-energy model.
Molecular dynamics.explanation: Propagates atomic motion over time using forces from a potential-energy model.
Molecular dynamics.example: A protein-water simulation integrates positions and velocities in femtosecond steps before structural averages are analysed.

Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.summary: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period and increases down a group because effective nuclear charge and shell number change.
Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.mistake: Do not answer Atomic and ionic radii trends from a memorised trend or name alone. Check the species, physical state, units, reaction conditions and known exceptions before drawing the conclusion.
Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.application: Atomic and ionic radii trends supports prediction and problem solving in senior-secondary chemistry, laboratory work, materials, environmental decisions and industrial chemical processes.
Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.explanation: Covalent, metallic and van der Waals radii are defined differently; ionic size also depends on charge and coordination. A board-ready explanation should connect the stated relationship with electronic structure, a measurable trend, a balanced transformation or laboratory evidence, and should name important exceptions instead of treating the rule as absolute.
Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.relationship: cation < parent atom < anion; isoelectronic radius decreases as Z increases
Classification and Periodicity: Senior S.example: Example: For O2-, F-, Na+ and Mg2+, all have ten electrons; radius decreases in that order as nuclear charge rises. Show the governing relationship, apply the stated conditions and finish by interpreting the chemical result.

History.summary: The periodic table developed as scientists searched for repeating patterns among the elements.
History.mistake: The periodic table was not invented in its final form by one person.
History.application: The history shows how pattern, prediction and new evidence improve scientific classification.
History.explanation: Early groupings by Dobereiner and Newlands led to Mendeleev's table; atomic-number evidence later produced the modern periodic law.
History.example: Example: Newlands noticed that properties repeated roughly every eighth element when elements were ordered by mass, an early sign of periodicity.

Undergraduate|Computational Chemistry|Mo.summary: Molecular dynamics propagates atomic motion over time using forces from a potential-energy model.
